prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a layered layout: a low table and its objects are nearest at roughly 0.3–0.8 m, the couch and visible person are about 1–2 m away, and the doorway, walls, ceiling, and rear room are roughly 2–5+ m away. Across the five frames, the couch shifts from the left toward the centre and then back left as the camera turns; the person moves from partly visible at the right edge to near the centre in frame 3, then leaves the field of view, while the large couch arm enters very close on the right in frame 5. It clarifies that the tabletop items are within the camera wearer's arm's reach, whereas the couch, person, and floor lamp are farther away; it also separates the lamp shade above and behind the couch from the nearer furniture despite their overlap in RGB. Absolute distances are uncertain, and the blown-out near foreground, smoothed object boundaries, person silhouette, thin lamp pole, and frame edges look unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies a couch in all five frames; a person at the right side of frames 1–2 and near the centre of frame 3; and small foreground objects including a potted plant, cup, and book clustered below and to the right of the couch in frame 1, with a plant and small chair region near the lower centre-left in frame 2. It makes the occlusion order clearer: the near table objects overlap one another and partly block the lower couch and person, while the person is partly cut off by the right border in frames 1–2 and more fully visible in front of the rear wall in frame 3. The couch is roughly 1–2 m from the camera, the labelled table objects about 0.3–0.8 m away and mutually separated by only a few tenths of a metre, and the person roughly 1–2 m away and within about 1 m of the couch; the map itself does not provide metric depth, so these estimates depend on RGB context. The masks show the camera turning past the person toward the couch in frames 4–5, but several labels and boundaries are unreliable: couch masks merge cushions and arms, the chair label is tiny, foreground objects disappear after frame 2, and the person mask in frame 3 is coarse.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects a sparse yellow body configuration only in frame 3, centred on the visible person's head and upper torso, with no dependable hand detections in any frame. The head landmarks face approximately toward the camera wearer, consistent with the frontal face in RGB, while the short shoulder/upper-body geometry places the person upright about 1–2 m ahead and below the ceiling fixtures; the map cannot establish eye gaze precisely. Its absence in frames 1–2 indicates that the partially occluded, edge-cropped person is not successfully localized there, and the absence in frames 4–5 matches the person moving out of view as the camera turns. The map adds joint-level localization that RGB alone makes harder to isolate, but the skeleton is extremely incomplete, provides no metric distance, cannot determine either person's arm reach, and the isolated lower horizontal yellow segment may be a false or misconnected detection.
